From Campus to Career

Choosing wisely and staying relevant in a changing world — an alumni conversation on career choices, industry readiness, AI-era skills, communication, integrity and lifelong learning.
26 September 2026 5:00 PM – 6:00 PM IST Online • MS Teams ME-RISE Foundation • MCE Hassan
“A degree opens the door. Real-world skills determine who walks through it.”
Distinguished Alumna
Shubha Girish
CSE 1993 • Technology Leader • 20+ years in technology
Executive Summary

What the session was really about

The conversation went well beyond placements. It examined how engineering students can make career choices with clarity, prove capability through real work, and remain employable as AI changes the nature of entry-level work.

Why Shubha's perspective mattered

Shubha spoke from both sides of the campus-to-corporate transition: as an MCE alumna who built a global technology career, and as a senior leader who has been involved in campus recruitment, talent development, enterprise systems and digital transformation.

Her central message was consistent throughout the session: students should focus on fundamentals, evidence of capability, curiosity, communication, integrity and adaptability rather than chasing every new trend.

Key discussion themes

  • The real gap between a degree and industry readiness.
  • Six major pathways after engineering.
  • Projects, internships and portfolios as proof of ability.
  • AI fluency without AI dependency.
  • Why communication is larger than language or accent.
  • Hackathons as learning laboratories, not just prize events.
  • Why “Why?” should precede major career decisions.

Career Architecture

Six broad pathways after engineering

The session framed careers as a set of choices to test, not a single irreversible decision made at graduation.

01

Industry Employment

Choose a domain, build relevant projects, pursue internships, tailor the resume to the role and compare offers by learning, team quality and growth — not salary alone.

02

Higher Studies

Start early. Build a strong academic profile, identify programmes and universities, prepare for tests, secure recommendations and articulate a clear statement of purpose.

03

Startups & Entrepreneurship

Begin with a real problem. Validate it with users, build an MVP, seek feedback, iterate and form a team with complementary skills.

04

Research & Deep Tech

Work with faculty, read and reproduce research, contribute to open source, present work and use the experience to test whether R&D or a PhD path fits you.

05

Freelance & New-Age Careers

Specialise, build a portfolio, learn pricing and contracts, communicate with clients and let completed work and testimonials establish your credibility.

06

Government & PSUs

Prepare systematically for competitive exams, study official notifications and previous papers, take mock tests and maintain a sensible backup plan.

Decision Quality

How to choose a path without being trapped by trends

Start with fit, not fashion

Your interests, strengths, values and preferred way of working matter more than whatever technology happens to be trending this month.

Optimise early years for learning

The first few years should maximise exposure, responsibility and skill-building. A career is a marathon, not a campus-placement sprint.

Talk to people ahead of you

Use the alumni network. Ask professionals what their real day looks like, what they enjoy, what they regret and what they would learn earlier.

Test before you commit

Internships, hackathons, research projects and freelancing let you experience a field before making a long-term decision.

Keep choices reversible.
Changing direction after learning more is not failure. It is informed adaptation.
AI & Future Readiness

What changes with AI — and what still matters

AI is reshaping coding, testing, documentation, analysis, design and engineering workflows. The answer is not to chase every new model. It is to become a strong engineer who knows how to use AI intelligently.

Strong fundamentals

Mathematics, algorithms, data structures, systems thinking and first-principles reasoning remain the foundation for understanding why systems behave the way they do.

AI fluency

Know how to use AI tools for research, productivity, coding and analysis — but do not confuse tool familiarity with deep understanding.

Data literacy

Read data, question it, identify signal from noise and understand the assumptions behind conclusions.

Human collaboration

Communication, teamwork, negotiation and ethics become more valuable as machines automate routine tasks.

Ownership

Build something, ship it, expose it to feedback and improve it. The world rewards evidence of execution.

Learning how to learn

Technologies will continue to change. The durable skill is the ability to learn new ones quickly and apply them with judgment.

Selected Discussion Moments

Questions that sharpened the conversation

“Technology changes every week. What should I learn?”

Do not attempt to master every trend. Build strong basics, strengthen learning ability, and demonstrate how you apply what you know.

“What should happen after a hackathon?”

Hackathons build teamwork, speed and product thinking. Not every idea must become a startup, but strong ideas deserve validation, iteration and possibly continued development.

“MBA immediately, or after work experience?”

The right answer depends on the purpose. Start with “Why do I want an MBA?” before deciding when to pursue it.

“Can AI eventually replace even human reasoning?”

AI capabilities are expanding rapidly, but regulated environments still require accountability, explainability, governance, privacy and human judgment.

“What about English and accent?”

Communication matters more than imitation. Improve language skills, but do not fake an accent. Clarity, listening, humility and authenticity are more important.

Action Framework

A practical career-readiness loop for students

EXPLOREKnow the options
LEARNBuild fundamentals
BUILDCreate evidence
SHOWPortfolio & repo
CONNECTMentors & alumni
REFLECTAsk “Why?”
ADAPTKeep moving
Final takeaway
Technology will continue to change. Careers will continue to change. What students can control is their ability to stay curious, build strong fundamentals, solve meaningful problems, communicate clearly, act with integrity and adapt continuously.
FAQ

Frequently Asked Questions

Start by understanding your interests, strengths and values. Then test possible paths through internships, projects, hackathons or conversations with alumni before making a major commitment.

There is no magic number. A few meaningful projects that you understand deeply are better than many shallow ones. Be ready to explain the problem, your specific contribution, failures, trade-offs and results.
It is increasingly valuable because it gives recruiters tangible evidence of your work. A portfolio can include code, demos, documentation, research, design work or problem-solving write-ups.
Use AI as a coach, research assistant and productivity tool. Ask it to explain, critique or generate alternatives — but verify the output and make sure you understand the underlying concept yourself.
No. Tools change quickly. Learn the fundamentals of your discipline, understand a small number of useful tools well, and develop the ability to learn new tools when the problem demands them.
Yes. Hackathons teach teamwork, rapid problem solving, pitching, technical execution and working under constraints. If an idea shows real potential, continue validating and improving it after the event.
Practise regularly, use transcription and AI-based feedback tools, read and speak often, and focus on clarity rather than accent. Strong communication is about being understood, not sounding foreign.
Curiosity, honesty, communication, problem-solving, ownership, humility, teamwork and the ability to explain your own contribution clearly are all important.
There is no universal answer. Clarify why you want the MBA, what career change or capability you expect from it, and then decide whether immediate study or some work experience better supports that purpose.
Yes. Career choices should remain reversible where possible. Changing direction after gaining evidence and experience is adaptation, not failure.
Learn how to learn. Curiosity, disciplined practice, reflection and the willingness to update your skills continuously are more durable than any one technology.
